# Chemical Bonding

## Core ideas and reasoning

Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, commonly formed by electron transfer between a metal and a nonmetal. An ionic crystal is an extended lattice, not a collection of isolated molecules. Covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs. Simple molecular substances may have strong covalent bonds within molecules but relatively weak intermolecular attractions, so low boiling points do not imply weak intramolecular bonds. Giant covalent structures such as diamond have strong bonds throughout the lattice. Graphite has layered bonding and mobile electrons, giving electrical conductivity unlike diamond. Metallic bonding involves positive metal centres and delocalised electrons, explaining conductivity and malleability. Ionic substances conduct when molten or in solution because ions can move, but not when solid. Methane is tetrahedral with angles about 109.5°; water is bent about 104.5° because lone pairs affect electron-pair repulsion. Diagrams are models and electron-dot counts must match valence totals and charges.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Explain why sodium chloride conducts when molten but not when solid.

In solid NaCl the ions are held in fixed lattice positions. When molten the ions move and carry electric charge.

### Example 2

Compare the bonding structures of methane and diamond.

Methane consists of small covalent molecules with weak attractions between molecules. Diamond is a giant covalent network with strong bonds throughout, requiring much more energy to disrupt.

### Example 3

State methane’s molecular shape and approximate H-C-H angle.

Tetrahedral, approximately 109.5°. Four bonding pairs around carbon repel into this arrangement.

## Check your reasoning
